content.text: I ran ~80 probes. Here are the precise rules.

findings.rule: Program name (`prog`) is derived at runtime from basename(argv[0]) — it is NOT hardcoded as "test4_executable". Every usage line and every "<prog>: error: ..." line must use basename(process.argv[1]) (Node: the script/exe name as invoked).
findings.evidence:
$ ln -sf /workspace/dataset/test4_executable /tmp/myprog; /tmp/myprog 2>&1 1>/dev/null
usage: myprog [-h] --a A --b B
myprog: error: the following arguments are required: --a, --b
(exit 2)

$ /tmp/myprog --help 2>/dev/null | head -2
usage: myprog [-h] --a A --b B

findings.rule:
Exact help text, on STDOUT, exit 0, nothing on stderr. Byte-exact:
"usage: <prog> [-h] --a A --b B

options:
  -h, --help  show this help message and exit
  --a A
  --b B
"
Note: heading is "options:" (not "optional arguments:"); 2-space item indent; exactly TWO spaces between "--help" and "show"; the "--a A" / "--b B" lines have no help text; single trailing newline.
findings.evidence:
$ ./test4_executable --help 2>/dev/null | od -c
0000000   u   s   a   g   e   :       t   e   s   t   4   _   e   x   e
0000020   c   u   t   a   b   l   e       [   -   h   ]       -   -   a
0000040       A       -   -   b       B  \n  \n   o   p   t   i   o   n
0000060   s   :  \n           -   h   ,       -   -   h   e   l   p    
0000100       s   h   o   w       t   h   i   s       h   e   l   p    
0000120   m   e   s   s   a   g   e       a   n   d       e   x   i   t
0000140  \n           -   -   a       A  \n           -   -   b       B
0000160  \n
0000161

$ ./test4_executable --help 2>&1 1>/dev/null | od -c
0000000            (empty)
$ ./test4_executable --help >/dev/null 2>/dev/null; echo "exit=$?"
exit=0

findings.rule: Every argparse error writes exactly two lines to STDERR (nothing to stdout) and exits 2: "usage: <prog> [-h] --a A --b B\n" followed by "<prog>: error: <message>\n". No trailing space anywhere, one trailing newline.
findings.evidence:
$ ./test4_executable 2>&1 1>/dev/null | od -c
0000000   u   s   a   g   e   :       t   e   s   t   4   _   e   x   e
0000020   c   u   t   a   b   l   e       [   -   h   ]       -   -   a

0000100   :       t   h   e       f   o   l   l   o   w   i   n   g    
0000120   a   r   g   u   m   e   n   t   s       a   r   e       r   e
0000140   q   u   i   r   e   d   :       -   -   a   ,       -   -   b
0000160  \n

(exit 2; stdout empty)

findings.rule: Missing-required message lists missing options in DECLARATION order (--a before --b), comma+space separated: both missing -> "the following arguments are required: --a, --b"; only --b missing -> "...: --b"; only --a missing -> "...: --a". Exit 2, stderr.
findings.evidence:
$ ./test4_executable
usage: test4_executable [-h] --a A --b B
test4_executable: error: the following arguments are required: --a, --b
(rc=2)
$ ./test4_executable --a 1
test4_executable: error: the following arguments are required: --b
(rc=2)
$ ./test4_executable --b 1
test4_executable: error: the following arguments are required: --a
(rc=2)

findings.rule: `--help` supports prefix abbreviation: `--h`, `--he`, `--hel`, `--help` all print help to stdout and exit 0. `-h` also works. Matching is case-sensitive: `--HELP` is NOT recognized. A string longer than the option (`--helpx`) is not a prefix and is therefore unrecognized.
findings.evidence:
$ for f in --h --he --hel --help -h --HELP --helpx; do ./test4_executable "$f"; done
[--h] rc=0 stdout="usage: test4_executable [-h] --a A --b B\n\noptions:\n  -h, --help  show this help message and exit\n  --a A\n  --b B"
[--he] rc=0 same help
[--hel] rc=0 same help
[--help] rc=0 same help
[-h] rc=0 same help
[--HELP] rc=2 stderr="test4_executable: error: the following arguments are required: --a, --b"
[--helpx] rc=2 stderr="test4_executable: error: the following arguments are required: --a, --b"

findings.rule: `--a` and `--b` cannot be abbreviated or extended: they must be given exactly (case-sensitive). `--A`, `--aa`, `--ab`, `---a` are all unknown option strings (they fall through to the leftover/extras list, so you normally see the missing-required error instead).
findings.evidence:
$ ./test4_executable --A 1 --b 2   -> rc=2 "test4_executable: error: the following arguments are required: --a"
$ ./test4_executable --a 1 --B 2   -> rc=2 "...required: --b"
$ ./test4_executable --aa 1 --b 2  -> rc=2 "...required: --a"
$ ./test4_executable --ab 1        -> rc=2 "...required: --a, --b"
$ ./test4_executable ---a 1 --b 2  -> rc=2 "...required: --a"

findings.rule: A bare `--` prefix with `=` (i.e. an empty option name) is AMBIGUOUS, not unknown: it matches all long options. Message: "ambiguous option: <original token> could match --help, --a, --b" (candidates in declaration order: --help, --a, --b; note `-h` is not listed). Exit 2. This error is raised during left-to-right token consumption, so it beats missing-required and unrecognized-args.
findings.evidence:
$ ./test4_executable '--=5' 2>&1 1>/dev/null | od -c
...  a   m   b   i   g   u   o   u   s       o   p   t   i   o   n   :       -   -   =   5       c   o   u   l   d       m   a   t   c   h       -   -   h   e   l   p   ,       -   -   a   ,       -   -   b  \n
(rc=2)
$ ./test4_executable '--='            -> "ambiguous option: --= could match --help, --a, --b"
$ ./test4_executable '--=abc' --a 1 --b 2 -> "ambiguous option: --=abc could match --help, --a, --b"
$ ./test4_executable --a 1 --b 2 '--=5'   -> "ambiguous option: --=5 could match --help, --a, --b"
$ ./test4_executable '--=5' --helpx       -> "ambiguous option: --=5 could match --help, --a, --b"

findings.rule: HELP DOES NOT ALWAYS WIN. Tokens are processed strictly left-to-right; -h/--help prints help and exits 0 the moment it is consumed. Therefore help wins over errors that are only detected at END of parsing (missing-required, unrecognized-arguments) regardless of position, but LOSES to any consumption-time error (invalid int value, expected one argument, ambiguous option) that occurs at an EARLIER token position.
findings.evidence:
help wins (rc=0, help on stdout):

$ ./test4_executable --c 3 --help
$ ./test4_executable --a 1 --b 2 --help
$ ./test4_executable --a 1 --b 2 --c 3 -h
$ ./test4_executable --a 1 --b 2 zzz -h
$ ./test4_executable --a 1 --b 2 -h 5
$ ./test4_executable --a 300 --help
$ ./test4_executable --help --a foo
$ ./test4_executable --help --a
$ ./test4_executable --helpx -h

error wins (rc=2, stderr):
$ ./test4_executable --a foo --help
test4_executable: error: argument --a: invalid int value: 'foo'
$ ./test4_executable --a=foo --help
test4_executable: error: argument --a: invalid int value: 'foo'
$ ./test4_executable --b foo --help
test4_executable: error: argument --b: invalid int value: 'foo'
$ ./test4_executable --a 1 --b foo --help
test4_executable: error: argument --b: invalid int value: 'foo'
$ ./test4_executable --a --help
test4_executable: error: argument --a: expected one argument

findings.rule: Even a range failure (bytes() ValueError, exit 1) loses to a later --help, because argparse finishes and exits 0 before main() runs. `--a 300 --help` prints help, exit 0.
findings.evidence:
$ ./test4_executable --a 300 --help 2>/dev/null; echo rc=$?
usage: test4_executable [-h] --a A --b B

options:
  -h, --help  show this help message and exit
  --a A
  --b B
rc=0

findings.rule: Unrecognized leftovers are reported as one message with the ORIGINAL tokens joined by a single space, in original argv order, regardless of whether they look like options, values, positionals, or `--`: "unrecognized arguments: <tok1> <tok2> ...". Exit 2.
findings.evidence:
$ ./test4_executable --a 1 --b 2 --c 3        -> "unrecognized arguments: --c 3"
$ ./test4_executable --a 1 --b 2 --c 3 --d 4  -> "unrecognized arguments: --c 3 --d 4"
$ ./test4_executable --a 1 --b 2 extra1 extra2 -> "unrecognized arguments: extra1 extra2"
$ ./test4_executable --a 1 --b 2 --c 3 zzz    -> "unrecognized arguments: --c 3 zzz"
$ ./test4_executable --a 1 zzz --b 2 -- yyy   -> "unrecognized arguments: zzz -- yyy"
$ ./test4_executable --a 1 --b 2 'hello world' -> "unrecognized arguments: hello world"
$ ./test4_executable --a 1 --b 2 --c=9        -> "unrecognized arguments: --c=9"
$ ./test4_executable --a 1 --b 2 ''           -> "unrecognized arguments: "  (message ends with a space then newline)

findings.rule: Unknown options do not affect where recognized options are read from; the unknown token (and a following non-option token it appears to consume) is simply collected, and its report order follows argv order. Position of the unknown option relative to --a/--b is irrelevant to the message content.
findings.evidence:

$ ./test4_executable --a 1 --c 3 --b 2   -> rc=2 "unrecognized arguments: --c 3"
$ ./test4_executable --a 1 --c --b 2     -> rc=2 "unrecognized arguments: --c"
$ ./test4_executable --c --a 1 --b 2     -> rc=2 "unrecognized arguments: --c"
